statement: A rectangle has perimeter 30 cm, and the length of each of its sides is a whole number of centimetres. How many different values can its area take?

choices.misconception: I also counted a 0 by 15 rectangle, with area 0, which is not a real rectangle.
I counted a 3 by 12 rectangle and a 12 by 3 rectangle separately, so I counted each area twice.
I counted every whole number from 1 to 15 as a possible side length.
I found the largest possible area, 7 x 8 = 56, instead of the number of different areas.

hints: What do the length and the width add up to?
Length plus width is 15. List the pairs of whole-number sides with the shorter side first, and check whether any two pairs give the same area.
The pairs are 1 and 14, 2 and 13, and so on up to 7 and 8, with areas 14, 26, 36, 44, 50, 54 and 56.

solutions.reliable: Half the perimeter is 15, so length + width = 15. With the shorter side first, the possibilities are 1 x 14, 2 x 13, 3 x 12, 4 x 11, 5 x 10, 6 x 9 and 7 x 8, with areas 14, 26, 36, 44, 50, 54 and 56. These are all different, so the area can take 7 different values. The transferable idea: read whether the question asks for a count of shapes, a count of values or a single value, and list without repeats.
solutions.elegant: The area a(15 - a) grows steadily as the shorter side a goes from 1 to 7, so the 7 choices of the shorter side give 7 different areas.

whyOnTest: The question asks for a count of different areas, so solvers who count ordered pairs or report the biggest area answer a different question.
author: Devansh Sanghavi
